title: Multi-config trace aggregate notes: cross-run latency summaries and hypotheses
content:
Goal:
Summarize an aggregate view of end-to-end trace samples collected across multiple runtime configs (gpu type, batch window, quantization profile, and cache warm/cold) and extract stable per-stage contributions at p50/p95/p99. The aim is to quickly identify reproducible regressions and isolate configuration-sensitive hot spots for follow-up action (bisect, microbench, tuning).

Context and test matrix:
- Workloads: chat-style generation (single-turn), prompt-only generation (long context prefix), and embed+generate hybrid.
- Models: open-vicuna-13B-ggml-quant (FP16 and int8 profiles), redwood-7b-optimized (float16).
- Hardware: A100-40GB, H100-80GB, and T4-staging nodes.
- Configs varied: batch_max_tokens (8, 64, 256), batch_wait_ms (0, 5, 25), kv_cache_enabled (true/false), quant_profile (fp16, int8-8bit), kernel_path: fast_matmul_v2 vs fallback.
- Sampling: 2K traces per config, sampled across normal traffic (not synthetic microbench).

Methodology summary:
- Each trace is decomposed into the canonical stages we use in the runtime: request-parse -> queue-enqueue -> batching-wait -> batch-dispatch -> kv-lookup -> kernel-exec -> token-emit -> postprocess -> response-egress.
- Times normalized to per-token (ms/token) for generation traces; embeddings reported as single-shot ms/request.
- We compute p50/p95/p99 per-stage and per-config, plus cross-config delta relative to the baseline (A100, batch_max_tokens=64, batch_wait_ms=5, kv_cache=true, fp16).
- We mark instability where coefficient of variation (CoV) of p95 across 10 200-trace bootstrap resamples > 0.15. Those results are flagged for more targeted capture.

High-level findings (short):
1) Kernel-exec dominates p50 (~60–75%) across warm-cached runs on A100/H100; however p99 shows much larger relative contributions from batching-wait and queue-enqueue when batch_wait_ms>20ms or on T4.
2) KV-cache cold starts cause a large p99 multipler (2.5–4x) localized in kv-lookup + kernel-exec due to cache population and memcopy spikes — more pronounced on H100 with int8 profile.
3) Int8 quantization reduced kernel-exec median by ~18% on A100 but increased p99 tail by ~22% vs fp16, suggesting more variance in emulated weight unpack / cold-path inflation.
4) Reducing batch_wait_ms to 0ms improves p50 but increases p99 for longer sequences: more microbursts and smaller batches increase queue contention and scheduling jitter.

Representative numeric slice (baseline vs two contrasting configs). All numbers are ms/token: p50 / p95 / p99. Values are stagewise; only key stages shown to keep doc readable.

Baseline (A100, batch_max_tokens=64, wait=5, kv=true, fp16):
- queue-enqueue: 0.7 / 2.3 / 4.1
- batching-wait: 1.8 / 3.5 / 6.9
- kv-lookup: 0.9 / 1.4 / 2.2
- kernel-exec: 6.3 / 10.7 / 18.6
- token-emit: 0.5 / 0.8 / 1.2
- postprocess+egress: 0.6 / 1.0 / 1.6
- E2E total: 10.8 / 19.7 / 34.6

H100 + int8 + kv cold (same batches):
- queue-enqueue: 0.6 / 2.6 / 6.0  (tail worse on H100 scheduling jitter)
- batching-wait: 1.7 / 4.2 / 8.8
- kv-lookup: 1.3 / 3.8 / 7.5  (cold population spike)
- kernel-exec: 5.1 / 16.2 / 30.0  (lower median but big tail)
- token-emit: 0.5 / 0.9 / 1.4
- postprocess+egress: 0.7 / 1.1 / 2.0
- E2E total: 9.9 / 28.8 / 55.7

T4 + batch_wait=25ms + small batch_max_tokens=8 (cost-constrained staging):
- queue-enqueue: 1.2 / 5.8 / 12.1
- batching-wait: 5.6 / 18.9 / 38.2
- kv-lookup: 1.0 / 2.0 / 3.4
- kernel-exec: 10.2 / 28.5 / 61.5
- token-emit: 0.6 / 1.5 / 3.0
- postprocess+egress: 0.8 / 1.6 / 2.7
- E2E total: 19.4 / 58.3 / 121.9

Interpretation and hypotheses (evidence + rough confidence levels):
- Hypothesis A: kernel exec variability on H100+int8 is largely due to two factors: a) weight unpacking path hitting a fallback kernel under certain sequence alignment patterns; b) interleaved DMA stalls when kv-cache population causes remote page faults. Evidence: tail samples often show a large contiguous kernel-exec subspan followed by a kv-lookup spike in same trace. Confidence: medium-high.
- Hypothesis B: Very long batching-wait tails on T4 are scheduler/backpressure artifacts — when many small batches accumulate the runtime scheduler serializes dispatch leading to big spikes at p99. Evidence: traces with latency spikes match periods of increased queue length and show long batch-dispatch gaps. Confidence: high.
- Hypothesis C: Setting batch_wait_ms to 0 reduces median by returning smaller batches immediately but increases p99 due to more frequent kernel scheduling; good for latency-sensitive low-SLO workloads but bad for 99s. Confidence: high.

Action items (next captures and short experiments):
1) Bisect kernel path: reproduce H100+int8 tail by running targeted microtrace with synthetic sequences that mirror the tail sample tokens and alignment. Add logging to kernel-selection path and instrument fallback triggers. Owner: Jonah Kim. Target: 2 weeks.
2) KV cold mitigation: run an experiment that pre-warms kv-cache for small fraction (1%) of requests and measure p99 improvement; if effective, add adaptive prewarm to routing policy. Owner: Luca Rossi. Target: 1 week for canary.
3) Scheduler tuning: run a T4-specific scheduling config that increases concurrency slots and short-circuits long batch windows. Compare p50/p95/p99 with and without. Owner: Sofia Martinez. Target: 1 week.
4) Dashboard: produce a small dashboard card that surfaces CoV-of-p95 across daily rolling window for each hardware/config pair and flags regressions > 20% automatically (so ops isn’t surprised). Owner: Aisha Patel (self). Target: 3 weeks.

Trace debugging tips and filtering queries (notes to self):
- Query examples (internal trace store):
  - find traces where kernel-exec > 2x median AND kv-lookup > 1.5x median within same token index -> likely cold-pop path.
  - filter traces with batching-wait > 10ms and batch_size < 8 -> indicates scheduler jitter causing long waits for small batches.
  - group by sequence_length_bucket (<=64, 65-256, >256) when computing p99; long-seq heavy tails often hide in >256 bucket.

Sample anomalous trace ids for pairwise inspection (sanitized):
- st-20260212-0a3f9c (H100-int8, kv cold): kernel-exec 29ms/token spike recorded at token idx 12; same trace shows kv-lookup 6.2ms next token.
- st-20251122-9c7d1b (T4, high batch_wait): batching-wait 42ms during a 7-token generation; scheduler gap observed.

Open questions / unresolved:
- Why is int8 increasing p99 on H100 but decreasing median? Need to confirm whether this is purely software (kernel selection) or memory subsystem related.
- Are there network stack interactions (egress path) that amplify kernel tails into larger E2E tails when downstream cold connections occur? We saw a few traces with postprocess+egress jumps correlated to ephemeral socket creation.

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducing an H100 tail locally:
- Use same docker runtime image as canary (runtime:release-2026-02-10).
- Use model build with int8-profile-2025-11.
- Run 1000 synthetic requests with sequence lengths sampled from the victim cohort (attached as a small csv in the linked artifacts).
- Capture full traces with debug logging enabled for kernel-selection, kv-cache miss logging, and DMA stall counters.

Summary sentence:
Cross-config aggregate traces show that median wins (kernel-optimizations, int8) can hide substantial tail risk introduced by cache coldness, scheduling policies, and fallback kernels; triage should combine targeted bisects, small prewarm canaries, and scheduler tuning to get p99s back under control without losing p50 gains.

Notes: rough draft; many of the numeric slices are sampling-based estimates and should be validated by targeted microbenchmarks before an SLA claim.

-- Aisha
